title: Of Offences Affecting the Public Health, Safety, Convenience, Decency and Morals
shortDescription: Offences that harm the public at large: public nuisance, spreading dangerous diseases, breaking quarantine, adulterating food and drugs, fouling water and air, rash driving and navigation, negligent handling of poison, fire, explosives, machinery, buildings and animals, obscenity, and unauthorised lotteries.

subHeadings.label: Public safety: roads, water and dangerous things

summary:
Chapter XV protects the community as a whole — its health, safety, convenience, decency and morals. Most of its offences do not need a particular victim to be harmed: they punish conduct that creates common danger or annoyance. It corresponds to Chapter XIV of the IPC (ss.268-294A), and the BNS keeps the IPC order: s.270 = s.268, s.271 = s.269, and so on up to s.297 = s.294A. Most offences are minor (commonly up to six months, or a fine), and the main changes are higher fine limits and the express mention of electronic content in the obscenity provision. The Gazette gives the chapter no sub-headings; its sections fall into five groups: public nuisance and public health (ss.270-273), food, drugs, water and air (ss.274-280), public safety (ss.281-291), punishment of nuisance (ss.292-293), and decency and morals (ss.294-297).

Section 270 defines public nuisance: an act or illegal omission causing common injury, danger or annoyance to the public or people in the vicinity, or necessarily causing injury, obstruction, danger or annoyance to persons using a public right. A nuisance is not excused because it brings some convenience. The general punishment is a fine up to ₹1,000 (s.292), and repeating or continuing a nuisance after a lawful injunction is punishable with up to six months (s.293). Sections 271 and 272 punish negligent (six months) and malignant (two years) acts likely to spread a disease dangerous to life, and s.273 punishes knowingly disobeying Government quarantine rules for any mode of transport.

Sections 274-278 protect food and medicine: adulterating food or drink to make it noxious for sale, selling noxious food, adulterating drugs so as to lessen their efficacy, change their operation or make them noxious (now up to one year, non-bailable), selling adulterated drugs, and selling one drug as another. Sections 279 and 280 punish fouling a public spring or reservoir and making the atmosphere noxious to health.

Sections 281-291 deal with public safety. Rash or negligent driving or riding on a public way (s.281) and rash navigation of a vessel (s.282) are punishable even if no one is hurt. Exhibiting a false light, mark or buoy to mislead navigators carries up to seven years and a minimum fine of ₹10,000 (s.283). Carrying passengers for hire in an unsafe or overloaded vessel (s.284) and causing danger or obstruction on a public way (s.285) follow. Sections 286-291 share a common pattern: rash or negligent acts with, and the knowing or negligent failure to guard against probable danger to human life from, poisonous substances, fire or combustible matter, explosives, machinery, buildings under demolition, repair or construction, and animals.

Sections 294-297 protect decency and morals. Section 294 defines obscenity — now expressly including content displayed in electronic form — and punishes selling, distributing, exhibiting, producing, importing, advertising or profiting from obscene material (two years; five years on repeat conviction), subject to exceptions for the public good (science, literature, art, learning), bona fide religious use, and ancient monuments and temples. Section 295 punishes selling or showing obscene objects to a child more severely. Section 296 punishes obscene acts and songs in public to the annoyance of others, and s.297 punishes keeping an office for an unauthorised lottery and publishing lottery proposals. None of the Chapter's offences is compoundable.
